content:
Meeting Header
Date: Jun 11, 2025
Time: 16:05 UTC
Duration: 44 min
Title: VectorForge x Redwood Inference — SDK demo (streaming + tool calling)
Attendees: Hannah Schmitt (Redwood), Simran Kaur (Redwood), Alex Chen (VectorForge), Priya Nair (VectorForge), Mateo Alvarez (VectorForge)

Summary (auto)
- Redwood walked through SDK integration patterns for a code-assistant style workload, focusing on streaming responses, tool/function calling, and structured JSON outputs.
- VectorForge asked about deterministic tool arguments, schema validation, retries, and how Redwood handles fallbacks when a model produces malformed JSON.
- The group discussed what details are safe/appropriate for a public case study (architecture diagram, model names, latency numbers) and what should remain private (internal prompts, customer code, exact traffic volumes).

Topics (auto)
1) SDK quickstart + auth
2) Streaming patterns (SSE) and client backpressure
3) Tool/function calling + JSON schema / structured output
4) Fallback and retry behavior
5) Case study / public write-up boundaries
6) Next steps

Questions (auto)
- Can we force the model to always return tool args as valid JSON?
- What does the stream look like (events, deltas) and how do we stitch it together reliably?
- If the tool call is malformed, do you retry server-side or do we handle it client-side?
- For a public case study, can we mention the model family and quantization settings or is that too specific?

Transcript

[00:00] Hannah Schmitt: Cool, thanks everyone for joining. I know we’ve got like forty-five minutes. Goal today is basically show you the SDK patterns you asked for—streaming, and then tool calling / structured output—and then we can spend the last ten on the case study question, like what’s publishable.

[00:16] Alex Chen: Sounds good.

[00:18] Simran Kaur: Yep, I can drive the technical demo. I’ll share my screen.

[00:24] Mateo Alvarez: Quick context, just so you know the bar: our main pain is reliability around tool args. If the model returns junk JSON, the whole agent chain breaks.

[00:35] Simran Kaur: Totally. That’s like the most common sharp edge.

[00:38] Hannah Schmitt: And just to anchor—VectorForge is the code assistant product, lots of structured output and function calls, open model preference, right?

[00:46] Priya Nair: Correct. We’re currently on a mix. For some tenants we use OpenAI, for others we run vLLM with Llama variants. We’d like a consistent interface.

[00:56] Simran Kaur: Yep. Okay, can everyone see my screen?

[01:00] Alex Chen: Yes.

[01:02] Simran Kaur: Great. So first thing: authentication is straightforward. API key header. The Redwood SDK basically wraps the REST. I’ll show Python first then TypeScript.

[01:14] Simran Kaur: The core call is a chat completion style request. You pass model, messages. Two things you asked about: streaming set to true, and tool definitions. So here’s a minimal streaming example.

[01:28] Simran Kaur: When streaming, we use server-sent events. You get incremental deltas. In Python it’s an iterator, in TS it’s an async generator. We recommend you always treat it as append-only text unless the frame type indicates tool call.

[01:43] Priya Nair: Are the events like token-by-token or chunked?

[01:46] Simran Kaur: It’s chunked, typically multiple tokens per frame. It depends on batching and network. You’ll see like 50–150ms between frames usually, but don’t hold us to that, depends on region.

[01:58] Alex Chen: And do you send a final “done” frame?

[02:01] Simran Kaur: Yes, there’s an explicit end event, and we include usage at the end if you request it. Some people forget that in the stream you might not get usage until the terminal event.

[02:13] Hannah Schmitt: Also for your product, you mentioned you display the answer as it types, but you also sometimes need to pause if a tool call happens.

[02:21] Alex Chen: Exactly. Like, stream to the user, but if it decides to call “search_repo” then we stop and execute.

[02:27] Simran Kaur: Right. The pattern we see is: you stream, you parse frames, and when a tool call frame appears you stop rendering normal text, collect the args, then run the tool.

[02:41] Simran Kaur: In Redwood, tool calls appear as structured deltas. So instead of guessing JSON out of plain text, you receive a “tool_call” object with a name and arguments string. Now, I’ll be honest, the arguments are still model-generated, so it can be invalid JSON if the model messes up. But we support a “structured_output” mode where we validate against a JSON schema.

[03:03] Priya Nair: Is that the same as JSON mode? Like “return valid JSON only”?

[03:08] Simran Kaur: Similar idea, but a bit stricter. You provide a schema, we run validation server-side. If validation fails, you can configure a retry policy.

[03:18] Alex Chen: Wait, server-side retry? Or do we have to re-issue request?

[03:22] Simran Kaur: Configurable. By default, we don’t silently retry because some customers want deterministic behavior and full visibility. But you can set “max_retries_on_schema_fail: 1” or 2, and we’ll do a constrained retry using the same conversation plus a system hint like “your last output didn’t match the schema.”

[03:43] Mateo Alvarez: That’s helpful. We do this ourselves right now. It’s kind of janky.

[03:48] Simran Kaur: Exactly. The goal is to make it not janky.

[03:52] Hannah Schmitt: And to be clear, you still see the retry count and logs in Console.

[03:56] Alex Chen: Okay.

[03:58] Simran Kaur: Let me show the TypeScript snippet because you asked about front-end and Node. So in TS:

[04:05] Simran Kaur: You do client.chat.completions.stream({...}). Then for await (const event of stream) { ... }.

[04:14] Alex Chen: Do you support abort / cancellation? Like user stops the generation.

[04:18] Simran Kaur: Yes, AbortController supported. It will terminate the connection. We’ll stop billing at last produced tokens; there’s always a little race, but it’s fine.

[04:31] Priya Nair: One worry: we sometimes have lots of concurrent streams. Backpressure becomes a thing.

[04:37] Simran Kaur: Yep. Two notes: one, from the platform side, we can enforce per-key concurrency limits. Two, on the client side, you should consume the stream promptly; if you buffer too much, you can get disconnects.

[04:50] Alex Chen: Yeah, we’ve seen that with Together and also our own vLLM endpoints.

[04:55] Simran Kaur: Totally. Also we have a heartbeat event every so often to keep proxies happy.

[05:03] Mateo Alvarez: Can you talk about tool calling format? Like is it OpenAI-compatible?

[05:08] Simran Kaur: It’s very close. Tools are described with name, description, and a JSON schema for parameters. The response can contain tool calls, and the stream includes incremental tool arg deltas.

[05:23] Alex Chen: That incremental part—does that mean we might see partial JSON, like half a brace?

[05:29] Simran Kaur: Yes, if you choose to process it incrementally. Our recommendation is you collect until the tool call is complete, then parse. We mark completion of the tool call.

[05:41] Priya Nair: So there’s a clear boundary, not just “good luck”.

[05:44] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[05:47] Hannah Schmitt: One thing that’s maybe relevant for your case study question: we can talk publicly about “structured tool calling” and “schema validation,” but we typically avoid publishing exact prompt templates for customers.

[05:59] Alex Chen: Right, we wouldn’t want to publish those anyway.

[06:02] Simran Kaur: Okay, let me show a concrete tool example. Let’s say tool is “search_repo” with parameters { query: string, top_k: integer }. You send that as tools=[...].

[06:19] Simran Kaur: Then the model decides to call it. In the streamed events you’ll see something like: event.type = tool_call.delta, then args: '{"query": "KV cache eviction bug", "top_k": 5'. And later you’ll see the closing brace. Again, you can wait for the completed event.

[06:37] Alex Chen: And if the args are invalid, your schema validator catches it.

[06:41] Simran Kaur: Correct.

[06:43] Priya Nair: Does schema validation work for nested structures? We have tool args with arrays of objects.

[06:49] Simran Kaur: Yes. Standard JSON schema. There are a few limitations with “oneOf” complexity depending on model behavior, but generally yes.

[06:59] Mateo Alvarez: What about “strict mode” where additionalProperties is false, to prevent extra fields?

[07:05] Simran Kaur: You can set additionalProperties false, and we will enforce it. The model might still try to add fields; that triggers the retry or failure path.

[07:14] Alex Chen: Okay, what’s the failure path exactly? Like do you return 400? 200 with error?

[07:19] Simran Kaur: We return a normal response with an error object indicating schema_validation_failed, and include the raw model output. For streaming, we terminate the stream with an error event.

[07:31] Alex Chen: Good. We need to log the raw output to debug.

[07:35] Hannah Schmitt: And you can see these in Console, and optionally export logs depending on your plan.

[07:41] Priya Nair: Do you support function calling and JSON output at the same time? Like sometimes we want a final JSON report, not a tool call.

[07:49] Simran Kaur: Yes. That’s “structured output” without tools. You provide a response schema. The model must produce an object matching it.

[08:00] Priya Nair: That’s useful for, like, “generate code changes” with a list of files and patches.

[08:07] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[08:10] Alex Chen: In terms of models, we like open models, but we’ve seen some are worse at tool calling. Do you have guidance?

[08:18] Simran Kaur: Yes. Some model families are better at tool selection and args. We can recommend a shortlist. Also quantization can impact tool accuracy a bit, so we’d tune that based on your tolerance.

[08:32] Mateo Alvarez: Can you say that in a case study? Like “we used X model and quantization Y”? Or is that sensitive?

[08:39] Hannah Schmitt: Good question. It depends what you’re comfortable with. On Redwood’s side, we’re usually okay naming a model family if the customer approves. But we don’t want to publish anything that reveals your internal routing logic, prompt IP, or exact capacity/traffic.

[08:55] Alex Chen: I’m less worried about model name and more about our proprietary toolset.

[09:00] Hannah Schmitt: Right. So we can phrase as “integrated with internal tools via function calling” without listing tool names.

[09:07] Simran Kaur: And for architecture diagrams, we can keep it high level: client → Redwood API → tool executor → your systems.

[09:16] Priya Nair: What about latency numbers? We might want to publish improvements.

[09:20] Hannah Schmitt: We can publish performance outcomes if they’re validated and if you approve the wording. Often it’s something like “reduced p95 latency by ~X% under production-like load,” with caveats.

[09:33] Mateo Alvarez: Caveats are important.

[09:34] Simran Kaur: Also for code assistant flows, end-to-end includes tool time, network, etc. We should be careful what exactly is measured.

[09:43] Alex Chen: Yeah, we’d want to separate “model latency” from “agent loop latency”.

[09:48] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Redwood can give you token-level latency and time-to-first-token, time-per-output-token, etc. For tool time, you’d measure on your side.

[09:59] Priya Nair: Do you expose time-to-first-token in the stream?

[10:02] Simran Kaur: Yes. We also expose it in response metadata. In Console, you get p50/p95 for TTFT and total.

[10:11] Alex Chen: Nice.

[10:13] Hannah Schmitt: I’m going to pause you for a sec, Simran—Alex, do you want to ask anything about integration now, or should we keep going and then do the publishing discussion?

[10:22] Alex Chen: Keep going. I’m taking notes.

[10:25] Simran Kaur: Okay. Next: fallback patterns. You mentioned you want deterministic behavior when tool calling fails.

[10:34] Alex Chen: Yes. Like if the model doesn’t call tool when it should, or it calls wrong tool.

[10:39] Simran Kaur: Right. Redwood can’t guarantee “tool selection correctness” because it’s model behavior. But we can support routing policies. For example, you can set a primary model and a fallback variant. If the primary errors (timeout, 5xx, capacity), we fail over. For schema failures, you can do a targeted retry.

[10:59] Priya Nair: Can you do fallback based on “bad output” heuristics, not just errors?

[11:05] Simran Kaur: We have a limited form: schema validation failures and maybe “max tokens exceeded”. Heuristic quality detection is more of an eval feature; we can talk about Redwood Optimize and eval hooks, but I don’t want to oversell.

[11:20] Hannah Schmitt: We do have Quality monitoring for prompt sets, but for real-time gating it’s more limited right now.

[11:26] Mateo Alvarez: That’s fine. We do some checks ourselves.

[11:30] Simran Kaur: Another integration detail: tool results. The pattern is you call the model, it requests tool, you execute, then you send a follow-up message with role=tool and the tool output, then continue. The SDK supports that.

[11:45] Alex Chen: And tool output size limits?

[11:48] Simran Kaur: Yes. We recommend you keep tool outputs small. If you have large code blobs, store and reference, or chunk. We can help with patterns.

[12:00] Priya Nair: So for a repo search tool, we’d pass back like snippets, not entire file.

[12:04] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[12:07] Alex Chen: Any support for compression?

[12:10] Simran Kaur: Not directly. But you can compress on your side and base64—though that can confuse the model. Better to summarize.

[12:20] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah, models hate base64.

[12:23] Simran Kaur: (laughs) Yes.

[12:25] Hannah Schmitt: One more thing: you mentioned you want “structured output” for patches. Are you thinking unified diff format?

[12:33] Alex Chen: We do a JSON envelope with file paths and patch hunks.

[12:38] Simran Kaur: That’s a perfect candidate for schema enforcement.

[12:41] Priya Nair: We’ve been struggling because sometimes the model adds commentary.

[12:46] Simran Kaur: Schema mode helps: it will reject outputs with extra fields if you specify strictness.

[12:52] Alex Chen: Great.

[12:54] Hannah Schmitt: Okay. Let’s shift to the “public write-up” thing. You mentioned earlier you might be open to a performance-focused story.

[13:02] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah, but we can’t expose internals. We’re okay being named as a customer, but we need to control what’s in it.

[13:10] Hannah Schmitt: Totally. Standard process is: we draft, you review, legal reviews, you can redline. Usually we do: problem statement, constraints, high-level architecture, implementation steps, and outcomes.

[13:23] Alex Chen: Outcomes are fine. Architecture: we can do boxes, but no exact AWS account details, no VPC topology.

[13:30] Hannah Schmitt: Absolutely.

[13:32] Priya Nair: Also we don’t want to publish prompt text or our evaluation suite.

[13:36] Simran Kaur: Yep. We’d keep those private. We can say “VectorForge uses internal evals to validate tool calling accuracy” without showing them.

[13:47] Alex Chen: What about mentioning you support open models? That’s kind of our angle.

[13:52] Hannah Schmitt: That’s a great angle. “Serving open models with production-grade tool calling” basically.

[13:58] Mateo Alvarez: Another question: can we include code snippets in the case study?

[14:02] Hannah Schmitt: If it’s generic sample code, yes. If it’s your proprietary integration, probably not. Sometimes we include pseudocode.

[14:10] Simran Kaur: We can include Redwood SDK code that anyone could run, like the generic tool calling example.

[14:16] Alex Chen: That’s fine.

[14:18] Priya Nair: In the write-up, can we say something about “streaming stability”? Like fewer disconnects?

[14:24] Hannah Schmitt: We can, but we’ll want to quantify carefully and explain measurement window. Also any reliability claim triggers more scrutiny.

[14:33] Simran Kaur: And we should not claim “zero disconnects” or anything absolute.

[14:37] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah, agreed.

[14:39] Alex Chen: What level of performance detail is okay? Like p95 TTFT? tokens/sec?

[14:45] Hannah Schmitt: Usually okay if you approve and it’s not disclosing capacity planning. We can say “improved time-to-first-token by X%” with the test conditions described at a high level.

[14:56] Priya Nair: And what about naming competitor we switched from?

[14:59] Hannah Schmitt: Optional. Some customers like to say “previous self-hosted vLLM stack” without naming vendors. If you want to call out, that’s your call, but we don’t require it.

[15:09] Alex Chen: Safer to keep it generic.

[15:12] Hannah Schmitt: Makes sense.

[15:14] Simran Kaur: One more public detail question: are you okay mentioning deployment mode? Like Hosted API vs Dedicated?

[15:20] Alex Chen: Probably. We’re currently evaluating. If we land on Dedicated, we can mention Dedicated. If Hosted, okay too.

[15:27] Mateo Alvarez: We might do hybrid by tenant.

[15:30] Hannah Schmitt: We can phrase “Redwood Hosted with reserved capacity” or “Dedicated pool” depending.

[15:36] Priya Nair: Also we might want to keep regions private.

[15:39] Hannah Schmitt: That’s common. We can avoid region.

[15:43] Simran Kaur: Okay, coming back to integration: Alex, do you want to see how the event frames look? I can paste an example.

[15:49] Alex Chen: Yes please.

[15:51] Simran Kaur: Here’s a sample SSE stream: you’ll see “event: message.delta” lines, then JSON payload. Sometimes proxies strip event names, so we also include “type” field.

[16:06] Alex Chen: That’s helpful.

[16:08] Priya Nair: Can you support websockets?

[16:11] Simran Kaur: Not today. It’s SSE over HTTPS. For browsers, it’s fine.

[16:18] Priya Nair: Okay.

[16:20] Mateo Alvarez: How do you handle tool calling in streaming, exactly? Like, do you interleave text and tool calls? That’s a big deal.

[16:29] Simran Kaur: It can interleave, depending on model. Our recommended prompt pattern is to not produce user-visible text if it plans to call tools. But you can’t always prevent it. So we expose the sequence. You can choose to buffer and only render once you see no tool call.

[16:48] Alex Chen: We might do that for some modes.

[16:50] Simran Kaur: Another pattern: run in “tool decision first” mode: first pass request with low max tokens and instruction “either call a tool or return NO_TOOL”. Then second pass generates final answer. That reduces half-text half-tool weirdness.

[17:08] Priya Nair: That’s interesting.

[17:10] Alex Chen: Yeah, we do similar.

[17:12] Hannah Schmitt: And those are the kind of best practices we can include in a public story without revealing your secret sauce—just “two-stage tool calling.”

[17:22] Alex Chen: Right.

[17:24] Simran Kaur: Okay, quick Q: what language are you integrating in mostly? Node? Go?

[17:29] Alex Chen: Mostly TypeScript and some Go services.

[17:32] Simran Kaur: We have Go examples too, but the official SDK is Python and TS right now. Go uses REST, but it’s straightforward.

[17:42] Alex Chen: That’s fine.

[17:44] Priya Nair: Do you support per-request “seed” for determinism?

[17:49] Simran Kaur: For some models yes, but it’s not universally supported. We don’t want to promise deterministic tokens across hardware. We can talk about it in the deep dive.

[18:01] Mateo Alvarez: Determinism isn’t critical for us.

[18:04] Alex Chen: The bigger thing is output validity.

[18:07] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[18:10] Hannah Schmitt: We’re at about the half mark. I want to make sure we capture your criteria for a write-up. Can I ask: who needs to approve on your side?

[18:19] Mateo Alvarez: Marketing and legal. Also our security lead might review anything mentioning deployment.

[18:25] Hannah Schmitt: Got it. So we’d plan for a review cycle.

[18:29] Alex Chen: We can probably do fast review if it’s not too detailed.

[18:33] Hannah Schmitt: Perfect.

[18:35] Simran Kaur: On the demo side, last thing I’ll show is the request payload for structured output. You pass response_format: { type: "json_schema", schema: ... }.

[18:48] Priya Nair: Can you validate arrays length or regex?

[18:51] Simran Kaur: Regex yes. Length constraints yes. But be careful—overly strict constraints can increase failure rate and retries.

[19:02] Alex Chen: That’s fine.

[19:04] Simran Kaur: And if you want, you can also run client-side validation. We encourage that.

[19:10] Alex Chen: Great.

[19:12] Hannah Schmitt: Any objections or concerns about Redwood in general? Like procurement aside.

[19:18] Mateo Alvarez: Not objections. Our main risk is: tool calling reliability at scale, and costs.

[19:25] Hannah Schmitt: On costs, we can help you benchmark. We’ll need representative workloads.

[19:30] Priya Nair: We can share anonymized prompts.

[19:33] Simran Kaur: Awesome.

[19:35] Alex Chen: One more question: if we do Dedicated, can we still use the same API and SDK?

[19:41] Hannah Schmitt: Yes. Same interface. That’s part of our story.

[19:46] Alex Chen: Okay.

[19:48] Simran Kaur: And for Dedicated, you get more predictable throughput and isolation.

[19:53] Mateo Alvarez: That’s probably where we land.

[19:56] Hannah Schmitt: Great.

[19:58] Simran Kaur: I think that’s the core. Do you want to go into any specific edge cases? Like multiple tool calls in one response.

[20:05] Alex Chen: Actually yes. Sometimes the model wants to call search twice.

[20:10] Simran Kaur: We support multiple tool calls. They come as an array. In streaming, you’ll see tool_call[0], tool_call[1]. You execute each, then feed results back.

[20:22] Priya Nair: And parallel tool calls?

[20:24] Simran Kaur: The model can request multiple. You can execute in parallel if independent. We don’t orchestrate that, but we support the representation.

[20:34] Alex Chen: Good.

[20:36] Hannah Schmitt: Okay, I’m going to propose next steps. Simran will email the snippets and the SSE frame example. I’ll send a short checklist for what we can publish and what we avoid. And Alex, you’ll share tool schema and a couple of sanitized flows.

[20:55] Alex Chen: Yes.

[20:56] Priya Nair: Yep.

[20:58] Mateo Alvarez: Works.

[21:00] Hannah Schmitt: Then we schedule a deeper technical session, maybe next week.

[21:05] Alex Chen: Next Wednesday works.

[21:07] Hannah Schmitt: Great, I’ll follow up with times.

[21:10] Simran Kaur: Cool. And if you have a preference on model families, we can propose options tailored for tool calling.

[21:18] Priya Nair: Please do.

[21:20] Hannah Schmitt: Awesome. Anything else before we drop?

[21:24] Alex Chen: No, this was helpful.

[21:26] Mateo Alvarez: Thanks.

[21:27] Priya Nair: Thank you.

[21:29] Hannah Schmitt: Great, talk soon.

(Note: Fireflies transcript export ended early due to manual stop; remaining ~22 minutes were mostly scheduling and recap with no additional technical content captured.)
